turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Lord, the rain. The car park is a lake entirely. Anyway, it's the legs has me in, doctor.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): The legs. What are they doing?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Cramps. Fierce ones in the calves, both of them, the left worse. Two months now. Of a night, nearly every night, and they wake me.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long, did you say? And does anything ease them?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm. Two months, yeah. If I get up and stamp about, or stretch the foot up, they ease, but sure then the night is gone.
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): And the terrier next door starts up then. White little yoke, barks at his own shadow.
[SEG0007] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's up on the landing with it most nights. I stay over a few nights in the spare room, so I hear her.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. Any swelling of the ankles or the calves?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No swelling. Grand in the daytime.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Redness or heat in either calf?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Not red, not hot.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No chest pain. I'm not short of breath either.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Waterworks or bowels, any trouble there?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Bowels grand, waterworks grand.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Operations in the past?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No, never had one. Of.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me what tablets you're on.
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Err. The water tablet, Mizartan for the pressure. I've high blood pressure this years. Metformine for me diabetes, and Omprazole for the acid.
[SEG0020] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The water tablet is Frusemide. Forty milligram, one in the morning, for the ankles. Every day, she doesn't miss it.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): And Mizartan, the strength?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Eighty, I think. White box.
[SEG0024] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Mizartan is eighty milligram, once in the morning. She's spot on with that.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Metformine dose?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Metformine, 500 milligram twice a day, with breakfast and with the tea.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the Omprazole?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Omprazole, twenty milligram, mornings. Five-ish years I've been on that one.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything from the shop besides?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Magnesium tablets. The girl in the shop said they're for cramps. I like that shop, they still say hello, not like the big place in town.
[SEG0031] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The magnesium is maybe four hundred milligram. I wouldn't swear to it. She takes it at night, most nights, though she misses the odd one.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): I hardly drink water. Three or four teas a day and a small glass with the tablets. My sister would drink a lake and be in the bathroom for it.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Smoke? Any alcohol?
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Never smoked in me life. A small sherry at Christmas, that's all.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): I used to walk miles in the post office. I'm retired out of that now. Don't walk much at all these days.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me read what the nurse wrote. Blood pressure one forty over seventy-seven. Pulse sixty-eight.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry, I misread that. The pressure today is one oh nine over seventy-seven. The sixty-eight was the pulse last time in March. Today's pulse is seventy-four.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your last pressure was one-forty, that was March too. Weight today is fifty-two kilograms.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Fifty-two. I was a stone heavier in the post office days. There was a canteen bun every Friday, that didn't help anyone.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): I've had a look at them. Soft both sides. No swelling, no redness. Pulses in both feet are there.

[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): So, two months of fierce cramps in both calves at night, the left worse, they wake you, and walking or stretching eases them. No swelling, no redness, no chest pain, no shortness of breath. Frusemide 40 milligram, Mizartan 80, Metformine 500 twice a day, Omprazole 20, plus the shop magnesium. Very little water.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): I was going to stop the water tablet today. Often that's what sets night cramps off.
[SEG0043] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The ankles come up fierce if she misses even a couple of days. The heart doctor told her to stay on it. And in March they said the potassium was a bit low.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. That changes it. We'll keep the Frusemide going. I won't stop it.

[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): I had thought of a magnesium blood level and an ECG on top. There's no chest pain, and the shop magnesium would muddy a level, so we'll leave those. Blood tests for the potassium this week. That's the plan.
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): Do I stay on the magnesium from the shop?
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stay on that one, but don't double it. And every night before bed, stretch the calves, the foot up towards you, hold it, both sides.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): And drink a bit more water. A glass with each meal, on top of the tea. Not a flood.
[SEG0049] person_1 (PATIENT): I can manage a glass with the meal. My cousin swears by bananas, two a day, and she's still driving at eighty-six, fair play to her.

[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bananas are fine if you fancy them. I'm not starting a potassium tablet. My impression is the cramps are coming from the water tablet and not drinking enough, and the potassium may be low. That's provisional, mind, until we see the bloods.
[SEG0051] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Will you want to see her after the bloods?
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Book back in with me in two weeks, when the results are in. They'll have the blood form for you outside.
[SEG0053] person_1 (PATIENT): Grand so. Two weeks, and I'll do the stretches. Mind yourself in that rain, doctor.

spec.situation: Older person with calf cramps at night for two months; takes a water tablet; drinks little water; magnesium from the shop; blood tests for potassium planned; stretching advice.

traps.happens: The transcript looks like speech-to-text: drug names are sometimes spelled wrongly ('Omprazole', 'Mizartan' for telmisartan, 'Metformine'), fragments and fillers appear ('Err', 'Of.', 'Mm.', 'Umm'), numbers are sometimes digits and sometimes words.
traps.label_rule: Medicine names are recorded as written in the transcript (name) with a normalized/generic name ONLY when the true drug is certain from context (a drug 'for the pressure' written 'Mizartan' is NOT certain enough: leave generic_name empty). Fragments and fillers are never facts.

traps.happens: The nurse reads vital signs aloud in spoken words ('one oh nine over seventy-seven', 'thirty-eight point three') and also gives a PRIOR value ('last time in March you were sixty-eight', 'your last pressure was one-forty'). Someone may also correct a reading.
traps.label_rule: vital_signs hold only the CURRENT measured values, written normally (109/77, 38.3, 52 kg). The prior value is NOT a vital sign; it is recorded in the weight/BP entry's own notes only if the schema allows, otherwise omitted. Every number must be exactly as said; never invent or round a value that was not said.

features: spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

bad.reason: Magnesium for cramps at night is supported; 400 mg is uncertain: caregiver says maybe and wouldn't swear to it.
bad.text: magnesium (dose=400 mg, frequency=at night, indication=cramps, status=currently_used, reported_by=caregiver)

omissions.text: No trouble with waterworks and no trouble with bowels were specifically asked and denied.
No previous operations/surgery was denied by the patient.

An initial plan to stop Frusemide because it can trigger night cramps was discussed, but after the caregiver said the ankles swell badly if she misses a couple of days and that the heart doctor told her to stay on it, the doctor changed plan and explicitly decided to keep Frusemide going and not stop it.
Caregiver reported that if Frusemide is missed for even a couple of days, the ankles swell badly, and that a heart doctor previously told her to stay on it.
Caregiver reported that in March potassium had been 'a bit low'.
The doctor considered but decided against checking a magnesium blood level and doing an ECG, because there was no chest pain and the shop magnesium would muddy a magnesium level.
The doctor advised not to start a potassium tablet.
Bananas were said to be fine if the patient fancies them.
The blood form would be available outside for the planned potassium blood test.
